label: Title
notes: Open by framing Chapter 3 as the construction chapter. The audience has already seen metric spaces and length spaces; now the problem is how to build new examples while keeping the distance function honest. Emphasize that every construction has a metric invariant attached to it.

label: Construction Toolkit
notes: The chapter is not a list of unrelated recipes. It is a controlled toolkit: local data, gluing, polyhedra, quotients, coverings, arcwise isometries, products, and cones. The recurring question is what the construction does to shortest routes and local neighborhoods.

label: Locality
notes: Use the jump metric as the first warning. Two metrics can agree locally yet disagree globally when one is not intrinsic. On the sampled circle, small chord jumps force travel around the circle, so the epsilon-jump distance remembers path length that the chord distance hides.

label: Gluing Closure
notes: Gluing should be presented as a metric closure operation, not merely as identifying points. Once a zero-cost edge is declared, triangle inequality propagates new upper bounds through every polygonal route, and the quotient distance is the largest semimetric compatible with those bounds.

label: Forced Shrink
notes: This slide slows down the previous heatmap. The declared relation is only A identified with C, but B to D shrinks because B can travel to A, cross the zero edge to C, then move to D. The lesson is that gluing has indirect metric consequences.

label: Polyhedral Links
notes: Polyhedral spaces package gluing in Euclidean pieces. A face point looks locally flat, an edge point has a link recording adjacent sectors, and a vertex can have a cone over a more complicated link. The link is the local data that tells us what kind of metric neighborhood we built.

label: Metric Graphs
notes: Metric graphs and word metrics are the one-dimensional and combinatorial face of the same idea. Edges are pieces, vertices are gluing sites, and distance is shortest route length. In a Cayley graph, the route count becomes algebraic word length with respect to chosen generators.

label: Quotients
notes: Quotients by isometries are safe when orbit representatives can be compared without creating fixed-point singularities. The orbit formula minimizes over representatives. Free translation actions preserve local geometry, while fixed-point actions compress directions into a singular quotient point.

label: Coverings
notes: Coverings are the local-isometry version of repeated geometry. Around a small enough arc in the base, the covering splits into separate sheets upstairs, and each sheet maps isometrically to the same base neighborhood. Deck transformations move sheets without changing length.

label: Arcwise Isometry
notes: Arcwise isometry is a length-structure statement, not an injectivity statement. The pleat map folds, so different source points can land together, but each path interval has the same length because the absolute slope is one on each linear piece.

label: Product Metric
notes: The product metric is the Pythagorean construction for length spaces. Distances in the factors combine by a square root formula, and a midpoint in the product splits into midpoint choices in each factor. The notebook's numerical check verifies this split.

label: Cone Metric
notes: The cone construction turns a base metric into angular data. The law of cosines controls distance between radial points, but the base separation is clipped at pi. When the angular gap is large enough, the shortest route can prefer the apex.

label: Inspection Lab
notes: The product and cone lab should be used as an inspection station rather than an extra theorem. Students can move parameters and watch the product midpoint balance, then increase base separation until the cone distance chooses the radial route through the tip.

label: Invariant Checklist
notes: The invariant checklist is the quality-control habit for constructions. For each recipe, ask which identity or inequality proves the metric has survived: triangle inequality, local agreement, orbit minimization, sheetwise local isometry, path-length preservation, product midpoint, or cone truncation.

label: Failure Modes
notes: The most common mistakes are assuming topology determines metric gluing, assuming local agreement determines global distance, assuming quotient maps are always locally regular, and assuming length preservation forces injectivity. These are exactly the traps the chapter's examples are designed to expose.

label: Summary
notes: Close by returning to the construction question. Chapter 3 gives ways to build spaces, but each construction comes with an audit: what happens to local neighborhoods, to shortest routes, and to metric formulas. That audit prepares the curvature chapters that follow.
